questions.stem: At 0.570c a particle of mass 1.00 × 10^-27 kilograms moves. What is its relativistic momentum?

Uses mass times light speed ignoring the actual velocity
Omits the velocity factor from gamma times mass times v

questions.stem: At 0.682c a particle of mass 1.00 × 10^-27 kilograms moves. What is its relativistic momentum?

options.misconception: Uses the classical kinetic-energy formula mv^2/2
Uses mass times light speed ignoring the actual velocity
Omits the velocity factor from gamma times mass times v

questions.explanation: Relativistic momentum is p = gamma times m times v = 1.367 times 1.00 × 10^-27 times 0.682c = 2.80 × 10^-19 kg m/s. The classical value m times v omits gamma and is too small; m times c ignores the particle's actual speed; gamma times m times c omits the velocity factor entirely.
questions.hint: Multiply the classical momentum by the Lorentz factor gamma.

questions.stem: A particle with rest energy 511 MeV moves at 0.300c. What is its relativistic kinetic energy?

Halves the kinetic energy a second time
Reports the total energy including rest mass

The classical half m v squared badly underestimates the result at relativistic speed, halving again is arbitrary, and gamma times rest energy is the total energy, not the kinetic part.

options.misconception: Uses the classical kinetic-energy formula mv^2/2
Halves the kinetic energy a second time
Reports the total energy including rest mass

questions.explanation: Relativistic kinetic energy is K = (gamma - 1) times the rest energy. Here gamma = 1.104, so K = 0.104 times 938 = 97.7 MeV. The classical half m v squared badly underestimates the result at relativistic speed, halving again is arbitrary, and gamma times rest energy is the total energy, not the kinetic part.
questions.hint: Subtract one from gamma, then multiply by the rest energy.
